cues.text: Welcome to Genetics and Evolution, our NEET Biology Unit seven foundation.
This recording uses an AI generated Marin voice.
A gene can have alternative forms called alleles, and a diploid individual
commonly carries two alleles at an autosomal locus.
Mendelian segregation describes separation of these alternatives during gamete
formation.
For an Aa by Aa cross with equal transmission, the expected genotypes are one
quarter AA, one half Aa and one quarter aa.
Under complete dominance and the other stated assumptions, the phenotype ratio
becomes three dominant to one recessive.
Dominant does not mean more common, healthier or evolutionarily superior.
These are probabilities across offspring, not a requirement that every set of
four children or seeds contain the exact ratio.
Genotype describes the allelic constitution, while phenotype reflects
observable expression in context.
This class introduces inheritance, molecular mechanisms and evolution, with
further pedigrees, sequence problems and mixed experimental applications
remaining.
For two independently assorting loci, an AaBb individual produces AB, Ab,
aB and ab gametes at equal expected frequencies.
With complete dominance at both loci and the usual assumptions, an AaBb by
AaBb
cross gives the familiar nine to three to three to one phenotype ratio.
This ratio is not expected automatically for linked loci, interacting gene
effects or every small sample.
A test cross pairs an individual of uncertain dominant genotype with an
appropriate homozygous recessive individual.
A monohybrid heterozygote test cross gives an expected one to one result,
while
the independent dihybrid test cross gives four equal classes.
Probability multiplication applies to independent events: the probability of
aa
at one locus and bb at another is one quarter times one quarter, or one
sixteenth, in the stated self cross.
Addition requires mutually exclusive outcomes or proper correction for
overlap.
State the parental genotypes, assumptions and requested outcome before
selecting a memorized ratio.
Incomplete dominance and codominance describe expression patterns rather than
disappearance of allele segregation.
In a familiar flower color example of incomplete dominance, the heterozygote
has an intermediate phenotype, and selfing it produces a one to two to one
phenotypic ratio alongside the genotypic ratio.
This does not mean parental alleles physically blend into a permanently
inseparable new hereditary material.
In codominance, both allele associated products are distinguishable in the
heterozygote, as in the familiar ABO AB comparison.
Neither pattern requires a dominant phenotype ratio of three to one.
A phenotype can also depend on environment, developmental stage and other
loci,
so dominance is a relationship within a specified comparison rather than a
universal ranking of alleles.
Distinguish an intermediate measured outcome from simultaneous expression of
two distinguishable products.
When a cross is given, first determine the gametes and genotypes, then apply
the stated expression pattern to infer the phenotype classes.
Multiple alleles means that more than two alternative alleles exist at a locus
in a population.
It does not mean one ordinary diploid individual carries every alternative at
that locus.
The elementary ABO model uses I A, I B and i.
I A and I B are codominant with one another and each is dominant over i in
this
account.
Group A can therefore be I A I A or I A i, group B can be I B I B
or I B i, group AB is I A I B and group O is
ii.
An I A i by I B i cross can produce A, B, AB and O offspring, each with one
quarter expected probability.
The phenotype alone may not uniquely identify parental genotypes.
This is the standard simplified inheritance model, not a complete treatment of
rare blood group variants or transfusion compatibility.
Keep population allele diversity, individual genotype and the medical use of
blood components separate.
Pleiotropy describes one gene influencing multiple phenotypic features, often
because its product participates in processes with several downstream effects.
It is different from polygenic inheritance, where multiple loci contribute to
variation in one measured trait.
A simplified additive model can give graded phenotypes as the number of
contributing alleles changes.
Familiar discussions of height or pigmentation illustrate why a trait need not
fall into only two obvious classes.
These traits also involve environmental and developmental influences, so an
elementary additive diagram is not a claim that one small set of alleles
precisely determines every person's appearance or outcome.
A continuous distribution does not by itself identify the exact number of
contributing genes.
Conversely, a gene with multiple effects need not produce a continuous
phenotype.
Avoid treating ancestry labels as a substitute for actual genetic evidence.
In questions, distinguish the number of loci, the number of traits affected
and
the role of environmental conditions before choosing between pleiotropy and
polygenic inheritance.
The chromosomal theory of inheritance connects Mendelian behavior with
chromosome transmission, associated with the contributions of Sutton and
Boveri.
Homologous chromosomes carry corresponding loci and separate during meiosis,
providing a physical basis for segregation in the elementary account.
Their orientation can support independent assortment of loci on different
chromosome pairs, while loci on the same chromosome can show linkage.
A chromosome contains many genes; it is not one giant allele for a single
visible trait.
Homologous chromosomes and sister chromatids are different relationships.
Homologues contain corresponding loci and may carry different alleles, while
sisters arise from replication of one chromosome.
A replicated chromosome still counts as one chromosome before centromeric
separation in the usual counting convention.
Genes, chromosomes and DNA molecules therefore require their own definitions.
Use the cell stage and the object being counted before inferring inheritance
or
ploidy from a picture.
The chromosome theory explains a mechanism, not a guarantee that every locus
follows an unlinked dihybrid ratio.
Sex determination systems differ among organisms.
In the familiar human chromosomal account, XX is associated with typical
female
development and XY with typical male development, with Y linked SRY signaling
important in the usual pathway.
Biological developmental variations exist, so the model is not a complete
description of every individual.
In birds, males are commonly ZZ and females ZW, reversing which sex is
heterogametic compared with the typical human example.
In the elementary honey bee haplodiploid account, unfertilized eggs develop
into haploid males and fertilized eggs into diploid females.
Queens and workers are both female; their caste difference is not explained
simply by one being haploid and the other diploid.
Haploid male bees produce sperm without an ordinary diploid reduction
division.
Do not import the human X and Y labels into every species.
Identify the organism, the gamete sources and the stated chromosomal system
before predicting offspring categories or chromosome numbers.
Linkage describes the tendency of loci on the same chromosome to be
transmitted
together.
Crossing over between nonsister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during
meiotic prophase can produce recombinant combinations.
Consider an AB over ab heterozygote with twenty percent recombination.
Under the usual equal reciprocal class assumptions, AB and ab gametes each
occur at forty percent, while Ab and aB each occur at ten percent.
The parental phase matters: an Ab over aB arrangement has different parental
classes.
Recombination frequency is recombinant offspring divided by total offspring in
a suitable informative cross.
Over short intervals, one percent recombination approximates one map unit, but
multiple crossovers can make observed recombination underestimate larger
distances.
A recombination fraction does not exceed one half in the ordinary two locus
comparison, even though map distances can be larger.
Physical DNA distance and genetic map distance are not identical units.
Always identify phase, cross design and the denominator before calculating a
percentage.
In the standard X linked recessive model, an individual with one X chromosome
can express an allele without a second corresponding X allele masking its
effect.
Typical haemophilia A and B and common inherited red green color vision
defects
illustrate this comparison, though not every bleeding or color vision disorder
has that inheritance.
A father passes his X chromosome to daughters and his Y to sons in the
ordinary
XY model, so direct father to son transmission of an X linked allele is not
expected.
A heterozygous mother and an unaffected father can have half their sons
affected under the simplified model; if male and female births are equally
likely, that is one quarter of all offspring.
Those denominators are different.
Pedigree inference requires enough family information and stated assumptions,
not one symbol in isolation.
Carrier expression and biological variation can complicate real cases.
These are inheritance exercises, not personal genetic risk estimates.
Thalassemias involve reduced production of particular globin chains, affecting
haemoglobin balance and red cell function.
The familiar beta thalassemia inheritance comparison is autosomal recessive,
while alpha thalassemia often involves different gene copy and deletion
patterns.
They should not all be reduced to one identical two allele example.
In a simplified recessive model, two heterozygous parents have one quarter
expected affected offspring, one half heterozygous and one quarter without the
specified allele, assuming the relevant genotype model.
A carrier state can have different effects from the more severe affected
condition; carrier does not automatically mean no detectable biological
feature.
Thalassemia is commonly described as a quantitative globin production defect,
contrasting with a structural haemoglobin variant such as the familiar sickle
cell substitution example.
Both affect proteins, but the molecular changes differ.
Keep inheritance category, gene or copy arrangement, amount of product and
clinical expression distinct.
This foundation explains the comparison rather than diagnosing an individual
from a blood related symptom.
Chromosomal disorders can involve chromosome number or structure rather than a
single small sequence change at one locus.
Nondisjunction is failure of appropriate chromosome separation during division
and can produce cells with abnormal chromosome complements.
The usual Down syndrome comparison involves an extra chromosome twenty one,
giving trisomy twenty one.
Some cases involve translocation or mosaic arrangements, so one karyotype does
not describe every case.
Turner syndrome is classically associated with forty five X, while Klinefelter
syndrome is commonly associated with forty seven XXY.
Their biological features and reproductive effects vary, and labels should not
be used to make absolute claims about every individual.
Aneuploidy differs from a complete extra chromosome set, which would be a
ploidy change.
A karyotype can reveal broad chromosome patterns but not every small mutation.
In an examination image, identify chromosome count, the particular chromosome
involved and any stated mosaic or structural context before assigning a name.
Evidence for genetic material came from different experiments addressing
different questions.
Griffith observed transformation in pneumococcal bacteria, showing a heritable
change associated with material from another bacterial preparation.
The experiment did not by itself chemically identify DNA as the transforming
substance.
Avery, MacLeod and McCarty connected transforming activity with DNA through
biochemical investigation.
Hershey and Chase used bacteriophages with different radioactive labeling of
DNA and protein to test which component entered bacteria and contributed to
subsequent phage production.
Phosphorus thirty two served as the familiar DNA label and sulfur thirty five
as the protein label in that design.
This does not mean every protein contains phosphorus free chemistry in all
contexts; the experiment relied on its particular materials and controls.
DNA is the main cellular hereditary material, while some viruses use RNA
genomes.
Keep the organism, the labeled substance, the experimental observation and the
conclusion separate.
One classic experiment is not a direct test of every possible biological
system.
A nucleotide contains a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and phosphate, while
a nucleoside lacks the phosphate component.
DNA ordinarily contains deoxyribose and the bases adenine, thymine, guanine
and
cytosine.
The two strands in the common double helix run antiparallel, with
complementary
A T and G C pairing.
A T pairs have two hydrogen bonds and G C pairs three in the familiar
structural account.
Covalent phosphodiester linkages form each strand's backbone; hydrogen bonds
do
not replace those backbone bonds.
Five prime and three prime refer to sugar carbon positions and define strand
orientation.
RNA commonly contains ribose and uracil instead of thymine and can form
complex
folded structures even when described as single stranded.
Chargaff type A equals T and G equals C relations apply to an ordinary
complete
double stranded DNA sample, not automatically to one isolated strand or every
RNA genome.
Identify the molecule and strand reference before calculating base
composition.
Long DNA molecules require organized packaging rather than remaining as
unrestricted straight strands.
In the elementary eukaryotic account, DNA wraps around histone protein
octamers
to form nucleosomes, with linker regions connecting neighboring units.
Further organization contributes to chromatin and the condensed chromosomes
visible during cell division.
A nucleosome is not one entire chromosome or necessarily one whole gene.
Histones interact with DNA and its charge, but chromatin structure is dynamic
and linked with accessibility and regulation.
The familiar euchromatin and heterochromatin comparison concerns relative
organization and activity tendencies, not a rule that every sequence in a
region has one fixed expression state forever.
Prokaryotic DNA occupies a nucleoid without a surrounding nuclear membrane and
is organized through its own proteins and topology; it is not simply naked DNA
with no organization.
Genome size, chromosome number and the number of protein coding genes are
different measures.
Do not infer biological complexity from chromosome number alone.
Semiconservative replication gives each daughter DNA duplex one parental
strand
and one newly synthesized strand.
Meselson and Stahl's density labeling experiment supported this model in
bacteria: after transfer from heavy to light nitrogen medium, the first
generation showed intermediate density DNA, and the next included intermediate
and light classes.
DNA polymerases extend a growing chain at its three prime end, so new
synthesis
runs five prime to three prime while the template is read in the opposite
direction.
At a replication fork, leading synthesis is relatively continuous and lagging
synthesis involves Okazaki fragments, but both use the same directional
chemistry.
Primase provides primers, helicase helps separate strands and ligase joins
appropriate backbone breaks after processing.
These enzymes are not interchangeable labels.
Replication copies DNA rather than directly translating a protein.
State whether a sequence is the template or the newly synthesized strand and
mark its ends before predicting the complementary product.
Transcription produces RNA using a DNA template in ordinary cellular gene
expression.
RNA polymerase reads the template in the three prime to five prime direction
and builds RNA five prime to three prime.
The coding DNA strand has the same written sequence as the RNA product when
both are shown five prime to three prime, except DNA T corresponds to RNA U.
For example, a coding sequence five prime ATG GAA three prime corresponds
to RNA five prime AUG GAA three prime in a suitable transcribed region.
The complementary template runs in the opposite orientation.
A promoter helps recruit the transcription machinery, while termination
processes define the end of transcription in the relevant system.
Not every transcribed RNA will be translated, because cells also produce
functional noncoding RNAs.
A gene's template strand cannot be chosen solely by whether it is drawn on the
top of a page.
Determine strand role, orientation and boundaries before converting a
sequence.
Many eukaryotic protein coding transcripts are first produced as precursor RNA
that requires processing before ordinary translation.
Splicing removes introns and joins exon sequences, while five prime capping
and
three prime polyadenylation modify many messenger RNAs.
An exon is a retained transcript segment, not necessarily a synonym for only
amino acid coding sequence, because untranslated regions can also be retained.
Alternative splicing can generate different transcript products from a locus.
In the elementary central dogma account, sequence information flows from DNA
to
RNA to protein.
Reverse transcription copies RNA into DNA in suitable biological systems; it
does not mean a protein sequence is directly read back into a nucleic acid
template.
Prokaryotic transcription and translation can be closely coupled, while
eukaryotic nuclear processing and export provide additional separation.
Not every RNA molecule receives identical modifications.
Identify the cell type, transcript stage and functional RNA class before
deciding what processing or information transfer is occurring.
The genetic code relates messenger RNA triplets, called codons, to amino acids
or termination signals.
A reading frame specifies which successive groups of three are read.
AUG commonly acts as a start codon and encodes methionine in the standard
account, while UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons.
The code is degenerate because several codons can specify the same amino acid;
this does not ordinarily mean one codon randomly specifies several amino acids
in the same standard system.
The code is nearly universal rather than absolutely identical in every
organelle and lineage.
A nucleotide substitution can be synonymous, missense or create a stop
depending on context.
An insertion or deletion not divisible by three can shift the downstream
reading frame within a coding region.
Do not infer the effect of a mutation from its size alone without its location
and sequence.
Codons belong to messenger RNA, while anticodons are complementary regions on
transfer RNA.
Translation converts the information in a suitable messenger RNA coding region
into an amino acid sequence.
Aminoacyl transfer RNA synthetases help attach the appropriate amino acids to
transfer RNAs using energy, establishing a key relationship between decoding
and the delivered amino acid.
Ribosomes coordinate initiation, elongation and termination.
Codon anticodon pairing helps position charged transfer RNAs, peptide bond
formation extends the chain and translocation advances the reading process.
The growing protein is not assembled by directly joining DNA bases to amino
acids.
In the familiar ribosomal account, A, P and E sites have distinct roles, with
the initiator transfer RNA placed in the P site during ordinary initiation.
Stop codons are recognized by release machinery rather than an ordinary
transfer RNA carrying a stop amino acid.
The ribosome reads messenger RNA five prime to three prime, while the
polypeptide grows from its amino toward its carboxyl end.
State the reading frame and termination boundary before counting translated
amino acids.
The bacterial lac operon provides an elementary model of regulated gene
expression.
Its structural genes lac Z, lac Y and lac A encode beta galactosidase,
permease and transacetylase in the familiar account.
A regulatory repressor can bind the operator and limit transcription when the
inducing signal is absent.
Allolactose, derived from lactose, interacts with the repressor and reduces
its
effective operator binding, permitting expression.
Lactose is therefore an environmental substrate connected with induction, not
a
molecule that physically replaces the whole promoter.
Strong expression also depends on glucose related regulation: low glucose
favors cyclic AMP associated CAP activation in the standard model.
The greatest expression is therefore expected when lactose is available and
glucose is low under the stated conditions, not merely whenever any lactose
molecule exists.
Promoter, operator, structural genes and the separately regulated repressor
gene have different roles.
Distinguish removal of repression from positive activation when interpreting a
regulatory table.
The Human Genome Project was an international effort launched in nineteen
ninety and completed in two thousand three, with a foundational human
reference
sequence among its major outcomes.
Its goals included sequencing, mapping, data analysis and attention to
ethical,
legal and social questions.
A reference genome is a shared research resource, not a claim that every
person
has exactly that sequence or that every region was resolved in the same way at
the original completion date.
Later sequencing and reference initiatives have filled gaps and broadened
representation, including pangenome approaches.
Genome annotation asks which sequences have particular functions and how they
are organized; reading bases does not automatically reveal every biological
consequence of every variant.
Historical textbook estimates of gene number or sequence coverage should be
recognized as dated descriptions rather than permanent constants.
Human genetic variation does not justify ranking populations as more or less
evolved.
Separate the project's historical accomplishment, the reference used and the
research question when interpreting genomic evidence.
DNA fingerprinting compares informative variable regions to distinguish
samples
or examine biological relationships.
Traditional accounts emphasize variable number tandem repeats and probe based
patterns, while many contemporary profiles use short tandem repeat markers
amplified and compared across several loci.
These methods do not require sequencing every base of a person's genome for an
ordinary profile.
Individuals inherit marker variants, so related people can share more alleles
without necessarily having identical multilocus profiles.
A reported match must be interpreted with the number of markers, population
frequencies, sample quality, contamination and alternative explanations in
mind.
Identical twins can share the usual inherited marker profile, illustrating why
a profile is not an infallible unique personal label in every context.
A DNA match alone does not establish when or how a biological sample arrived
somewhere.
For an examination problem, identify the marker type, the comparison and the
parental contribution rather than treating every dark band as an entire gene
with a known phenotype.
Origin of life questions concern how nonliving chemical systems could have
contributed to the emergence of living organization, distinct from explaining
later diversification of established life.
Chemical evolution ideas associated with Oparin and Haldane proposed stages in
the accumulation and organization of organic materials.
The Miller Urey experiment generated organic compounds, including amino acids,
under a particular simulated set of conditions.
It did not create a living cell or prove that the actual early atmosphere
exactly matched its gas mixture.
Laboratory synthesis establishes chemical possibility under specified
conditions rather than a complete historical reconstruction.
RNA world ideas propose important early roles for RNA related information and
catalysis, but they are hypotheses studied alongside other evidence and
models.
Experiments rejecting ordinary spontaneous generation in present day settings
do not automatically settle every question about ancient prebiotic chemistry.
Distinguish observation, experimental conditions and historical inference.
The origin of life's first systems and evolutionary changes within populations
are connected topics with different evidential questions.
Darwin's contribution emphasized descent with modification and natural
selection as explanations for the diversity and adaptation of life.
Individuals vary, some variation is heritable, and differences in survival and
reproduction can change the contribution of variants to later generations.
Fitness in this context concerns reproductive contribution in a particular
environment, not a universal measure of strength, intelligence or moral worth.
Natural selection acts on existing phenotypic variation while populations
change across generations.
It does not instruct an individual to produce exactly the mutation it needs.
The modern synthesis connects evolutionary reasoning with Mendelian
inheritance
and population genetic processes, including mutation, recombination,
selection,
drift and gene flow.
Environment matters because a variant's consequences depend on the conditions
in which it occurs.
A useful trait is not evidence that evolution planned toward a goal.
Keep the source of variation, the sorting process and the resulting frequency
change separate when explaining an adaptation.
Fossils include preserved remains, impressions and traces that provide
evidence
of organisms and environments from the past.
Preservation is selective, so the record is incomplete and biased toward some
habitats, tissues and conditions.
Relative dating uses relationships such as stratigraphic order, with
geological
disturbances and context taken into account.
Radiometric approaches estimate ages of suitable materials using isotope decay
and appropriate assumptions; not every fossil is directly dated by the same
method.
A transitional fossil can combine features informative about evolutionary
relationships without being the direct ancestor of every later species in a
group.
Absence from one sampled layer is not proof that an organism never existed
anywhere.
Multiple lines of geological and biological evidence help reconstruct
histories
and test competing interpretations.
Evolutionary sequences are branching histories rather than obligatory ladders
from simple to superior organisms.
In a question, identify the specimen, the surrounding material, the dating
method and whether the conclusion concerns relative order or an estimated
numerical age.
Homologous structures share an evolutionary origin even when their present
functions differ.
The basic skeletal organization of vertebrate forelimbs provides a familiar
comparison across walking, flying and swimming adaptations.
Analogous functional similarities can arise independently, as in some wing
comparisons between insects and vertebrates.
The level of comparison matters: bird and bat forelimb bones are homologous as
inherited tetrapod structures, while their particular flight adaptations
include independently evolved features.
Convergent evolution describes independent acquisition of similar traits in
separate lineages under suitable pressures, whereas divergent evolution
emphasizes differences accumulating from a shared ancestral pattern.
Superficial resemblance alone cannot establish the exact relationship.
Vestigial structures can retain modified or reduced functions; vestigial does
not mean every such structure must be completely useless.
Compare developmental organization, anatomical connections and other evidence
rather than matching only one function.
A structure can participate in more than one useful comparison depending on
which feature and historical level the question specifies.
Embryological similarities can provide evidence of shared developmental
organization and evolutionary relationships.
This does not mean an embryo literally passes through the adult forms of every
ancestral species.
Historical oversimplifications of recapitulation should not replace actual
comparative evidence.
Molecular comparisons use homologous DNA, RNA or protein sequences to assess
relatedness and infer histories with suitable models.
Greater similarity can support closer common ancestry in a properly chosen
comparison, but rates vary and not every sequence evolves at the same speed.
Similarity at one short region should not automatically be treated as a
complete species tree.
Shared derived characters and concordant evidence across sources strengthen
inference.
Branch rotation in a tree does not change the relationships encoded by its
connections, and an unscaled branch length is not automatically elapsed time.
Distinguish the data, the inferred branching pattern and the uncertainty.
Molecular and developmental evidence complement fossils and anatomy rather
than
making every other source of evidence irrelevant.
Mutation can create new sequence variants through changes such as
substitutions, insertions, deletions or larger alterations.
Recombination reshuffles existing allelic combinations and can generate new
genotypes without necessarily creating a new allele at each locus.
Mutations are not directed toward what an organism will need in the future,
although mutation rates and mechanisms can differ across sites and
environments.
Their effects can be harmful, neutral or beneficial depending on the
biological
context.
A change outside a protein coding region can still affect regulation, while a
change within a coding region need not alter an amino acid.
Heritable variation is relevant to evolution only through the appropriate
transmission route; not every somatic change is passed to offspring in
ordinary
sexual reproduction.
Selection, drift and other processes then influence the fate of variants in
populations.
Do not equate the appearance of variation with its inevitable spread.
Identify origin, inheritance and population dynamics as separate steps.
Selection can be compared through how reproductive success relates to a
variable phenotype.
Directional selection favors variants toward one end of a distribution and can
shift its mean.
Stabilizing selection favors an intermediate range and can reduce variation
around it.
Disruptive selection favors contrasting extremes relative to intermediates and
can increase separation in the distribution under suitable conditions.
These descriptions are models, not proof that every measured trait follows a
fixed bell curve or that disruptive selection automatically creates two
species
in one generation.
The phenotype must have an appropriate heritable basis for a sustained
evolutionary response in the stated model.
Environmental changes can alter which values are favored, so an optimum is not
a permanent universal target.
A graph of phenotype frequencies differs from a graph of reproductive success
against phenotype.
Read axes, compare generations and identify the mechanism rather than choosing
a selection label solely from one curve's color or height.
Industrial melanism in peppered moths is a familiar example connecting
heritable variants with environmental conditions and differential survival,
including effects of camouflage and predation in the standard account.
It does not mean soot directly instructed every moth to grow a genetically
appropriate dark form.
Antibiotic resistance provides another comparison: resistant bacterial
variants
can increase when treatment conditions disproportionately remove susceptible
bacteria.
Resistance can involve new mutations, existing variation or acquisition of
genetic material, depending on the case.
The antibiotic does not deliberately teach bacteria which specific mutation
will be useful, and it is the microbes rather than the patient's body that
become antibiotic resistant in this biological sense.
These examples demonstrate context dependent differences in success, not a
rule
that one variant is superior in every possible environment.
Clinical antibiotic use requires appropriate care; the lesson explains the
evolutionary mechanism rather than a treatment plan.
Separate the variant's origin from the selective environment and subsequent
frequency change.
Gene flow is movement of genetic variants between populations through
successful reproductive contributions.
Organisms can migrate without producing offspring, so physical movement alone
does not always establish gene flow.
Pollen transfer and seed movement can connect plant populations, while
movement
and reproduction connect many animal populations.
Gene flow can introduce alleles into a population and often reduce genetic
differences between connected populations, but the outcome depends on
migration
patterns, selection and other processes.
It does not automatically improve adaptation or erase every population
difference.
Reduced gene flow can permit divergence, especially when other forces and
reproductive barriers contribute, but geographic separation alone is not an
instant guarantee of speciation.
A change in allele frequencies can have more than one explanation, so examine
the evidence for reproductive exchange rather than assigning every change to
mutation or selection.
Distinguish the population boundary, the source of migrants and whether their
alleles actually enter later generations.
Genetic drift is random change in allele frequencies caused by sampling across
generations and related demographic events.
Its effects are generally stronger in smaller populations, where chance
differences in reproductive contribution can have large proportional
consequences.
An allele can be lost or become fixed without being favored by natural
selection.
A founder effect occurs when a new population begins from a limited sample of
a
source population.
A bottleneck sharply reduces population size and can leave a surviving sample
that differs genetically from the earlier population.
Both can alter diversity, but neither guarantees improved adaptation.
A rare allele is especially vulnerable to chance loss, while a harmful allele
is not automatically immune to random increase when other forces permit it.
Drift concerns population sampling rather than individuals intentionally
changing their genotypes.
Compare population size, sampling history and evidence for differential
fitness
before deciding whether a frequency change is best explained by drift,
selection or their combined action.
The Hardy Weinberg principle provides a reference model for allele and
genotype
frequencies under specified assumptions.
For two alleles with frequencies p and q, p plus q equals one.
Under the equilibrium model, expected genotype frequencies are p squared, two
p
q and q squared.
The assumptions include random mating and negligible effects of selection,
mutation, migration and drift in a sufficiently large idealized population.
If a recessive phenotype corresponds exactly to aa and occurs at frequency
zero
point zero nine in equilibrium, q is zero point three and p is zero point
seven.
The heterozygote frequency is two times zero point seven times zero point
three, giving zero point four two.
The recessive phenotype frequency is not q itself in this example.
A departure from expected proportions does not uniquely prove natural
selection; other assumptions can fail.
State whether the observation is an allele, genotype or phenotype frequency
and
whether equilibrium is justified before applying the formula.
Adaptive radiation describes diversification from a common ancestral lineage
into forms associated with different ecological opportunities or roles.
Darwin's finches provide a familiar example, with differences in traits such
as
feeding structures interpreted within a branching history and environmental
context.
Australian marsupials illustrate another standard textbook comparison
involving
varied ecological forms.
A radiation does not mean one individual transforms into several species
during
its lifetime or that every branch has exactly the same evolutionary rate.
Similar ecological forms in separate radiations, such as some marsupial and
placental mammal comparisons, can illustrate convergence rather than immediate
close ancestry of the matching forms.
Ecological opportunity, inherited variation, geographic context and
reproductive divergence can interact.
Not every increase in species number must be labeled adaptive radiation
without
evidence for the relevant ecological diversification.
Read a tree as a set of branching relationships and compare the traits
independently, rather than arranging all living forms on a ladder from
primitive to advanced.
Human evolution is reconstructed through fossils, archaeological evidence,
comparative anatomy and genetics.
Humans share common ancestors with other living apes; we did not descend from
the chimpanzees living today.
Hominin history includes branching lineages rather than one universally agreed
straight ladder in which every named fossil species is a direct ancestor of
the
next.
Australopithecine and early Homo comparisons, Homo erectus and later human
lineages illustrate changes and diversity across time, with details revised as
evidence improves.
Bipedal locomotion, brain characteristics, diet, tools and social behavior did
not all appear in one simultaneous jump.
Homo sapiens originated in Africa, and later population histories include
movement and interactions with other human lineages.
Ancient DNA has provided evidence of some such interactions, including
Neanderthal contributions to many present day genomes.
No living population is an earlier evolutionary stage of another.
Distinguish evidence, branching relationship and uncertainty rather than
treating one skull feature or cultural label as a measure of human worth.
Genetics and evolution questions often combine several levels of explanation.
An allele can affect a molecular product, a phenotype can depend on
environment
and several loci, and population frequencies can change through more than one
process.
Begin by defining the organism, cross, locus, sequence orientation or
population being analyzed.
Use probabilities with the correct denominator, not as guaranteed outcomes for
every small family.
Mark template and product strands before transcription or translation
calculations.
In evolutionary reasoning, separate the origin of variation from the processes
